Metropolitan Hotel
Nanking, Jan. 29, 1937
Dear Family:
Flew up here from Shanghai this morning for a conference on
International Airmail.
As you know this is the new capital - new since
1927 when the seat of
the Government was moved from Peking.
This is a modern hotel built and operated by the China Travel
Service which is a tourist bureau with Government complex.
It will be
interesting sometime to come back to Nanking many years from now and
see what has really happened.
China is growing more nationalistic all
the time - the Sian scuffle not withstanding - and here especially you
evidence of the national idea on every side.
The manifestations are
frequently extremely immature and the enthusiasm for the slogan China
for the Chinese takes on something of the Collegiate lack of perspective.
Even the dry subtile humor which usually saves John Chinaman from
Rotarian excuses seems to desert him.
It's a case of more national less
rational.
In other words in this respect - there are few others - the
Chinese are like the Japs - unable to laugh at themselves.
Nanking is an enormous city in area - it is los Angeles with
a wall around it - but in an
attempt to make people build expensively
up instead of economically out they limit
amount of ground to be
owned by one citizen
to two mow - about one-third of an acre.
result you see a new house here and there with no garden or even yard -
just house.
There is room for thousands upon thousands of such.
parently they hope to make sprawling Nanking look like congested
Shanghai where the "foreign devils" have built a great city in a small
At one time they talked of pulling down the city wall for more
room but that was just one too many for the most Rotarian of the
Nationalists.
This Hotel used to have a large sign out in front writ-
ten in English METROPOLITAN HOTEL but the Nationalists had the sign re-
moved and also severely criticised the management for having English
initials "M H" on the silverware.
That's funny too because tonight at
dinner there was a Russian Jazz band, proverbial Swiss manager,
of Frenchmen, one of Germans, another of Dutchmen and & scattering of
English, Americans, Japanese
and Chinese.
The only man among those
known to me was an American Associated Press reporter
wearing the perpetual frown of those charged with the responsibility
telling the world what the Chinese officials themselves do not know,
namely, what they are going to do next.
In front of the hotel runs the long wide new Chung Shan RoAD
(Central Mountain - Dr. Sun Yat Sen's posthumous name) edged with patch-
es of sidewalk in spots but mostly mud.
this road moves the usual
cavalcade of Chinese traffic the wheel that squeaks
Shrieking wheelbarrows whose axles belie
our New England auxis axiom
the loudest is the
wheel that gets the grease."
Man pulled carts, donkeys, motor cars,
rickshas and a host of spitting pedestrians all
of whom move along
with that utter and
complete disregard of the other fellow which is the
predominate characteristic of the Chinese.
John Chinaman is for him-
self and he doesn't like to give way to rules of traffic or regulations
which may be all right for the other man but do not apply to him.
The
ricksha puller gets out in the road well away from the curb and
there
he stays
threading his way through
the wandering pedestrians with crys
and shouts which make no impression on his noise unmindful compatriots.
You remember Joseph Pulitizer had a sound proof room
built to rest his
jaded nerves and nearly went loco when a cat "stamped" around his room.
Well if Joe had been blessed with a yellow epidermis and
slant eyes
he could have moved his office to a boiler factory and really concen-
trated.
Now there has been
added to the
confusion
motor bus - and here again is illustrated the
shairference

Page 2
Chinese for the rights of the other fellow.
I saw a bus stop in front
of a large crow - the bus already
every single one of the crowd got in.
Every seat was taken and each
sitter sitting bolt upright while in front of him between his knees
and the back of the seat ahead stood as many as could squeeze in. The
aisle was packed solid. A bus designed for sixteen was carrying not
less than sixty and no
doubt after six months of such overloading
operators will notify the German manufacturers that the busses have
worn out,
are no good and they won't meet the next maturing payments.
Such is Chinese consideration for
the other passenger, owner, manufact-
urer, rules, etc.
They would do the same thing with airplanes if it
not for the
foreign management.
Every airplane has
capacity which is certified in the
case of American planes by
U. S. Department of Commerce, Aeronautics Division.
Every passenger
and all cargo is weighed.
Instructions not to overload are exact and
uncompromising.
The pilot checks cargo and his weight report and re-
fuses to take off if the gross weight is over the safe limit. Harry
Smith who used to fly for Chiang Kai-shek tells an amusing story.
had orders to fly his tri-motor Ford on a long trip over bad country
so he decided to take plenty of gas and had to cut down his passenger
list to six.
Knowing the inclination of the Chinese
took great pains to explain to the No. I, who was a Secretary of Chiang
Kai-shek's,
that there could only be six
passengers.
Harry said he
that the instruction was indubitably clear.
So forceful had
ne made nis order that the following morning he didn't "cruise his cabin"
until he had taxied down to the end of the field.
Then he looked around.
and there were seven passengers.
He was so mad that he didn't trust
himself to speak so he walked through the cabin and got outside to cool
Presently the No. 1 followed and blandly asked if anything was
wrong. Harry said "Didn't I tell you only six passengers?"
Whereupon
No. 1 said there were only six.
Harry counted seven but the No. l
pointed to a big fat Buddha-looking placid oriental in the back
and said "on he isn't a passenger, he's just a servant."
Another time an American pilot flying a large Government
owned plane was given a load of silver
going with the shipment kept piling cases into
the cabin until the
pilot made them a long speech telling them that it wasn't safe to
overload and finally made them take all
the cases out.
being no scales the pilot himself lifted each case,
guessed its weight,
marked it down and set the case over to one side to be put in the plane.
Several times he caught his traveling companions (who were very anxious
to load all the silver) slipping a case which he hadn't "weighed" in
the other door of the plane.
After much explaining and no end of con-
fusion he thought he had the situation in hand.
Some silver was sent
back by the guards who brought it, the custodians were put on board
and the pilot took off.
The ship was overloaded and staggered off
near the end of the runway, the tail hit a pile of rocks, damaging
the tail surfaces,
washing away the tail-skid and nearly wrecking the
the airplane vibrating badly and sliding around the
sky the pilot was afraid to make a landing
with such a heavy load so
continued on to his destination too worried and busy
to enjoy the
fright and discomfort of his passengers who had been responsible for
their predicament.
The pilot got down at Kweiyang all right and we
had dinner together that night with Missionaries.
When the Mission-
aries prayed before chow the pilot whispered to me that he was well
up on them in both fervor and amount of praying that day.
Later he
repaired the damaged tail surfaces with new fabric and dope,
fashion-
ed a tail-skid from a wooden poppy field plough
and with a few lusty
cheers for free silver, missionaries and opium took off in a cloud of
Debby and
the girls are in Hongkong where I plan to join them
on Feb. 4th to spend Chinese New Year (The Nationalists call it Spring
Festival) because, in spite of the adoption by the National Government
of our calendar,
the Chinese still celebrate the old lunar New Year
and there's no use trying to get anything accomplished during the
festivities.
AS EVer,
